entry.evidence: Despite increased terrestrial inflows to fjords due to climate changes, we know little about the effects on the ecosystem, especially biogeochemical cycling.

sequences.source_document: Erga et al. 2023, Biogeochemistry 162:113–140 (publisher XML text)

steps.action: State the aim: how seston multielement concentration and stoichiometry of a deep fjord respond to environmental conditions over an annual cycle, with emphasis on land-fjord and fjord-coast interactions and microbiota.
steps.quote: The main objective of this study was to investigate how seston C:N:P:O:Si:Ca:Mn:Mg:Fe:K:Na:Cl:S:Cu:Zn elemental concentration and stoichiometry of a deep coastal-fjord system

steps.action: Sample one station (Brekke, outer Sognefjord) with Niskin bottles and a CTD (temperature, salinity, density, oxygen, chl a fluorescence) on nine cruises, with Winkler oxygen and AOU.
steps.quote: at selected depths using 2.5 L Niskin bottles, at nine time-points between 27 June 2012 and 31 July 2013

steps.action: Calibrate the CTD temperature sensor before use, and calibrate CTD salinity against AutoSal measurements referenced to IAPSO Standard Sea Water.
steps.quote: Salinity was calibrated by measuring salinity of samples collected from the deepest sampling level on each cast using a Guildline 8400 AutoSal

steps.action: Measure dissolved nutrients (autoanalyzer; NH4+ by microplate fluorometry), flow-cytometric counts of prokaryotes, viruses and phytoplankton, and SPM elemental composition at five depths by WDXRF on PC and GF/F filters.
steps.quote: Samples for SPM elemental analysis were filtered in triplicate onto 0.6 µm pore size Poretics polycarbonate (PC) filters (47 mm)

steps.action: Check the analytical premises: chloroform blanks below nutrient levels, at least three blank filters per batch and regular reference standards for WDXRF, and cross-calibration of particulate P on GF/F versus PC filters.
steps.quote: Particular P was also measured on GFF filters and cross calibration with PC filters showed consistent results (r2 = 0.9).

steps.action: Take wind data (eKlima, Ytterøyane lighthouse), current speeds (NorKyst800 model) and freshwater runoff data (NVE) from external sources.
steps.quote: Data on water runoffs to the inner SF were kindly given by the Hydrology Department at Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE)

steps.action: Identify from the hydrography the conditions met during the year: a brackish summer surface layer from snowmelt runoff, and an inflow of dense Atlantic water across the sill in late autumn 2012, followed by upwelling.
steps.quote: which indicates an inflow and descent of dense AW across the sill in late autumn 2012

steps.action: Report the nutrient, chl a, prokaryote, virus and phytoplankton distributions, including whole-column NH4+ depletion in March and an Emiliania huxleyi bloom in May–June 2013.
steps.quote: Notably, NH4+ was depleted over the whole water column in March.

steps.action: Establish across nine cruises a vertical pattern in particulate elements: major elements (C, O, N, Si, Ca, Cl, P, S) peak at 5 m, and Fe, Mg, Mn, K, Zn, Cu peak in the basin (Tables 1–2, Fig. 6).
steps.quote: High concentrations of Mn were only found in the basin layer

steps.action: Ordinate elemental composition (PCoA, betadisper) and relate it to environmental and microbial constraints by db-RDA with permutation anova.
steps.quote: The only variables that significantly affected the sample distribution were temperature, salinity and Synechococcus abundances (anova, p < 0.005).

steps.action: Rerun the db-RDA with only microbial constraints and with only nutrient and oxygen constraints, and compare the sample partitioning with the full-constraint ordination.
steps.quote: appeared very similar to the ordination constrained by all variables

steps.action: Correlate freshwater runoff with surface particulate element concentrations to argue for terrestrial influence (Table S3).
steps.quote: there was a positive correlation between freshwater runoff and surface concentrations of particulate S, C, P, Mg, and Ca (Table S3)

steps.action: Infer an ascent velocity of basin water from the October–December salinity increase and compare it with published eddy and upwelling velocities.
steps.quote: indicates ascent velocities of 17 m day−1, which are in accordance with those for eddies (20–40 m day−1) and coastal upwellings (17 m day−1)

steps.action: Derive expected settling times and horizontal transport distances for phytoplankton and clay from published sinking speeds, and from them the expected fate of particles (retention or flushing).
steps.quote: SPM in the form of phytoplankton would need more than 80 and 500 d to reach sill depth and fjord bottom, respectively

steps.action: Check the inferred resuspension against scanning electron microscopy of filters from 1220 m, which show clay and silt particles.
steps.quote: In August and February clay/silt particles were seen on the filters from 1220 m, confirming such bottom-up circulation process.

steps.action: Compare dissolved N:Si:P ratios (whole column, basin and upper 200 m) with Brzezinski's 16:16:1 and with earlier NCC and Norwegian Sea values, and conclude that fjord basins act as silicate reservoirs.
steps.quote: which differ slightly from the classical N:Si:P = 16:16:1 ratio often used as criteria for stoichiometric nutrient balance of diatom-dominated systems

steps.action: Re-estimate the ascent rate independently from the July silicate displacement and find it matches the salinity-based estimate.
steps.quote: This gives an ascent rate of 17 m day−1, consistent with the speed found at an early stage of the upwelling

steps.action: Compare NH4+ levels with the Oslofjord and the oligotrophic Northeast Atlantic.
steps.quote: with levels (0–1.85 µM) similar to those found in the Oslofjord

steps.action: List rival explanations for the NH4+ depletion during upwelling (NH4+-deprived AW inflow, adsorption onto clay or silt, organic ligand binding) and for other N conversion processes, without testing them.
steps.quote: could be due to inflow of NH4+ deprived AW, removal of NH4+ cations by adsorption onto ascending and negatively charged clay/silt particles

steps.action: Estimate the algal share of particulate C at 5 m by applying a POC/chl a ratio of 81 from the Samnangerfjord to the measured chl a.
steps.quote: we find that microalgae on an annual basis may contribute with 4.7 µM C of the total particulate carbon (13.9 µM) at 5 m

steps.action: Compute depth-specific annual-mean stoichiometry (Table 3) and compare it with the Redfield ratio, nearby fjords, soil microbiota and bacterial C:N:P and C:O values.
steps.quote: none of the particulate C:N:P annual means at specific depths (Table 3) were close to the oceanic Redfield ratio (106:16:1)

steps.action: Propose explanations for the high N:P and low C:N at depth (heterotrophic microbes, faster C and P decomposition, N-enriched clay, redox processes at the sediment–water interface).
steps.quote: Together, these facts suggest contribution from heterotrophic microbes, faster microbial decomposition of C and P than N

steps.action: Relate particulate elements to salinity and temperature (Fig. 8), and compare inter-element correlation matrices between upper and bottom layers (Table 4).
steps.quote: Elements in the stable bottom layer (800–1220 m) had higher numbers of strong correlations (r2) than at shallower depths

steps.action: Attribute the C–Ca and C–S correlations to calcite and organosulfur-producing microorganisms, and the S–Fe–Cu–Zn correlations to metal sulfide release from sediments.
steps.quote: probably related to calcite (CaCO3) and organosulfur producing microorganisms

steps.action: Calculate from earlier studies the particulate Si and Ca that diatom and coccolithophorid blooms can contribute, and set these against the measured totals.
steps.quote: it can be calculated that diatom and coccolithophorid (dominated by Emiliania huxleyi) blooms in Norwegian fjords

steps.action: Compare Si–Mg–K–Ca–O correlations between the basin and the upper layer, and match them to the expected vertical distribution of clay and biogenic silica.
steps.quote: which fits well with the vertical distribution of clay particles

steps.action: Compare K:Mg:P, Mn and K/Mg ranges with the eastern tropical North Atlantic, the southern North Sea and other Norwegian fjords.
steps.quote: which is approximately 10 times higher than values measured in the eastern tropical North Atlantic

steps.action: State rival sources for the bottom Mn enrichment (resuspension of MnO2-rich sediments versus Mn reduction, diffusion and reoxidation) and for Cu and Zn (clay adsorption versus anthropogenic release), leaving both open.
steps.quote: Another possibility is Mn reduction in the sediments, followed by diffusion of Mn2+ and reoxidation in bottom waters

steps.action: Keep the depth-specific ranges and the overall average seston stoichiometry as a reference relationship, noting that the overall N/P is consistent with Redfield.
steps.quote: Based on annual means at specific depths seston elemental stoichiometry (molar) were within the ranges

tree.answer: Seston multielement stoichiometry varying with depth and season in a deep fjord
Yes for element concentrations (WDXRF); ascent rates and algal C share are inferred
Describe the stoichiometry and relate it to environment and microbiota
Rivals named only post hoc (NH4+ depletion, Mn source, low C:N, Cu/Zn source)
No distinct predictions derived for the rivals
Conditions found (seasonal cycle, AW inflow, upwelling), not set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nine cruises over 13 months at one station; seasons repeat once
Analytical controls, constraint-subset db-RDAs, SEM check, independent ascent-rate estimate
Stoichiometric ranges and average kept; mechanisms left as likely or possible

end.claim: Annual-mean seston stoichiometry in the Sognefjord ranges C37–65N8.4–31P1Si2–7.2… by depth, giving an overall average C55N16P1Si3.6Ca3.4O16Fe0.74Mn0.51Zn0.33S0.21Cu0.08Cl1.7Na0.68Mg0.71K0.37; no depth-specific C:N:P matches Redfield, though the overall N:P does.

decisive_move.sentence: The WDXRF multielement analysis of SPM at five depths on nine cruises, using two filter types, produced every concentration and ratio the claim rests on.

gates.evidence: Sampling was designed as a descriptive annual cycle (§1 ¶5), with no hypothesis directing it. The stoichiometric claim faced only analytical controls (blanks, reference standards, P cross-calibration, §2.2 ¶4) and ordination checks. Mechanistic attributions are stated as 'likely', 'could' or 'probably' and are not tested against outcomes that could have failed them, except that SEM confirmed clay at 1220 m (§4.1 ¶3). Nothing was fixed before the data.

imports.item: Wavelength dispersive X-ray fluorescence (WDXRF) spectroscopy adapted for marine particulate matter
Flow cytometry with SYBR Green-I DNA staining for counts of prokaryotes, viruses and phytoplankton
Scanning electron microscopy of filters (Zeiss Supra 55VP, JEOL)
PCoA, betadisper and distance-based redundancy analysis (R packages cluster, ape, vegan)

novelty_claims.quote: [...] data on spatiotemporal variations of seston multielement stoichiometry in the Sognefjord
As far as we are aware such deep water multielement relationships are novel for coastal areas and has value as reference far beyond its geographical [...]

limits: Limits of the study as reported: one station, one annual cycle, nine cruises. The datasets are not public (available on request). Several supporting results are 'data not shown': bottom current speeds, the 250 m halocline samples, per-sample C/N/P ranges, and the March C:N:P. Standard errors are given for concentrations but not for the stoichiometric ratios, so the resolution of the headline estimate is only partly characterized. Sub-claims and their statuses: deep basin as silicate reservoir (best_explanation); ascent velocity of 17 m/day (estimate, no uncertainty given, but independently re-estimated); 34% algal C at 5 m (estimate built on a borrowed POC/chl ratio); alternative N-sequestration mechanisms, calcite and organosulfur sources, Mn from resuspension or redox cycling, and Cu/Zn from clay or anthropogenic sources (all suggested, not tested; at most best_explanation). Inference from the text: betadisper p = 0.02 is reported as 'not significant', and the Fig. 7 caption swaps panels c and d relative to the text, so the robustness reading of the db-RDAs is uncertain. The many r2 values in Table 4 carry no correction for multiple comparisons. Composition: natures_repetition is the closest fit, since correlations are fitted across naturally recurring seasonal conditions and the conditions cannot be set; the walk is largely descriptive, and no rival is excluded. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown.

disagreements.target: Classic Redfield C:N:P atomic ratio 106:16:1 (Redfield et al. 1963)
disagreements.support: Depth-specific annual means depart strongly (N/P 8.4 at 5 m, 21–31 below; C/N 1.6–6.5), while the time-and-depth average gives Redfield N:P but low C:P and C:N.
disagreements.quote: [...] both time and depth, however, the particulate N:P ratio became equal to Redfield (16:1)

disagreements.target: Classical N:Si:P = 16:16:1 nutrient balance for diatom-dominated systems (Brzezinski 1985)
disagreements.support: Regression of dissolved nutrients gives N/P 12.7 and Si/P 12.5 overall, and 8.6:28.4:1 in the basin.
disagreements.quote: which differ slightly from the classical N:Si:P = 16:16:1 ratio

disagreements.target: Literature on SPM elemental stoichiometry that focuses on Redfield C:N:P
disagreements.support: The authors argue from ecological stoichiometry that elements beyond C-N-P are needed to identify particle types and origins, and measure 15 elements.
disagreements.quote: information on essential elements beyond C-N-P are prerequisite to better ascertain which particles are involved and their origin

alternatives_considered.chosen: GF/F filters for C and N; PC filters for O, Si, Ca, Mn, P, Mg, Fe, K, S, Cu, Na, Cl, Zn
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Single filter type (P also measured on GF/F)
alternatives_considered.reason: to compensate for analytical interference from the elemental composition of the filters themselves

alternatives_considered.chosen: db-RDA with all constraints, plus separate nutrient-and-oxygen and microbial-and-chl a constraint sets
alternatives_considered.reason: To look at the individual effects of dissolved inorganic nutrients and the microbial community respectively

alternatives_considered.chosen: Annual averages for each element at each depth (Table 3)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Per-sample ratios across dates and depths; overall time-and-depth average
alternatives_considered.reason: To unravel systematic differences between water layers with respect to seston elemental stoichiometry

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Inflow of NH4+-deprived AW; adsorption onto clay or silt particles; complex binding within organic ligands

alternatives_considered.chosen: Resuspension of clay particles and MnO2-rich sediments (called 'likely' in the abstract)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Mn reduction in sediments, diffusion of Mn2+ and reoxidation in bottom waters
alternatives_considered.reason: none given for the preference; the alternative is said to be consistent with elevated Mn/Fe ratios

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Clay adsorption of Cu and Zn versus release from anthropogenic sources (industry, aquaculture)
